oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Mental Language and Life's Self-Movement
oai_dc:dc.dc:creator: Oliva, Mirela
oai_dc:dc.dc:subject: Mental Language, Life, Trinity, Gadamer, Aristotle, Augustine, Aquinas
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: In this paper, I argue that the notion of mental language entails a conception of thinking as a vital operation within the self-movement of life. I focus on Gadamer's re-elaboration of the medieval Christian doctrine of the inner word, showing its roots in Aristotle's vision of life as self-movement. In the first part, I argue that Gadamer proposes the notion of mental language in opposition to language instrumentalism and mechanistic science. In the second part, I show that this notion rests on the Greek, especially Aristotelian, idea of life as self-movement and of thinking as a self-relating act. In the third part, I focus on the Trinitarian conception of inner word (verbum interius), as it was developed by Augustine and Aquinas, and re-elaborated by Gadamer. I contend that the vital aspect of the Trinity is crucial to understanding the emergence of language.
oai_dc:dc.dc:source: Journal of Gadamer Studies; Vol. 1 No. 2 (2026): Language, Virtue, Friendship and Communal Practice
